questions.q: When does Python create the value of a default argument?
options: Every time the function is called without that argument
Once, when the def statement runs
The first time the function is called
When the module is imported, before any def runs
explanations: That's how many people expect it to work, and why the bug surprises them. The default is not rebuilt per call.
Right. The def statement evaluates the default once and stores that object on the function.
Close, but it happens earlier: at definition time, before any call.
Defaults are evaluated as each def runs, in order. Nothing happens before the def line itself.

questions.q:
Predict the output:

def add(name, team=[]):
    team.append(name)
    return team

add('pikachu')
print(add('eevee'))
explanations: That would be true if each call got a fresh list. It doesn't; both calls share one.
Right. The first call left 'pikachu' in the shared default list, and the second call appended to it.
append adds to the end, so the order is the order of the calls.
Nothing here is the wrong type. The code runs; it just shares state.

questions.q: Which default value is safe to use?
explanations: A list can change, so every call that uses the default shares and changes it.
A dict can change, so it has the same problem as a list.
Right. None can't be changed, and it clearly means "not passed", so you can build a fresh object inside the function.
A set can change, so it has the same problem as a list.

options: An error: the INSERT leaves out id
explanations: That would mean the default was computed once and reused, which is how Python treats a default argument, not how Postgres treats a column default.
Right. The column default runs for each inserted row, so each team gets its own id.
The INSERT added two rows, and each has an id. There are no missing ids to leave out of the count.
Leaving a column out of an INSERT is exactly when its DEFAULT is used. Nothing here is required and missing.
